strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: formalizing and enforcing group-level fairness constraints directly within the optimal transport framework for matching problems.

The conceptual progression is logically sound and comprehensive, moving from an exact projection algorithm (FairSinkhorn) to two principled relaxations: a convex penalized formulation and an amortized cost-learning formulation via bilevel optimization.

The theoretical analysis provides solid statistical guarantees, specifically establishing an expected sample complexity rate of order n^{-1/2} for the penalized entropic formulation and bounding out-of-sample fairness deviations for parameterized ground costs.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is restricted to small-scale synthetic 2D datasets (Gaussians and concentric circles with sample sizes as small as 20 to 50 points per subgroup). The absence of real-world matching datasets (such as school assignment or job recommendation benchmarks) limits the practical assessment of the proposed methods.

The manuscript contains noticeable drafting and formatting flaws: Section 5 has duplicate consecutive subsections titled 'Approaches and Metrics' (5.1 and 5.2) with repeated text, missing reference markers (appearing as question marks in Appendix C), and overlapping layout elements in Figure 7.

The experimental comparison for out-of-sample reusability only reports runtime and fairness variance, omitting the evaluation of out-of-sample transport cost and utility degradation on unseen test splits.

The theoretical bound in Theorem 4.4 carries an exponential dependence on the inverse entropic regularization parameter, which significantly degrades the sharpness and practical value of the guarantee in low-entropy regimes.

strengths: Formulates a natural and mathematically rigorous notion of group fairness for optimal transport (OT) matching problems through target mass constraints across subgroups.
Derives FairSinkhorn, showing that exact group fairness constraints can be integrated into the classic dual scaling framework via block-wise Bregman projections.

Provides meaningful theoretical analysis: establishes an O(1/\sqrt{n}) sample complexity bound for fairness-penalized entropic OT (Theorem 4.2) showing no degradation in parametric rate relative to standard entropic OT, alongside a uniform deviation bound for the cost-learning approach (Theorem 4.4).
Introduces two complementary relaxation strategies (convex penalization for optimal Pareto trade-offs and bilevel cost learning for amortized, reusable matching on unseen test samples).
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is strictly limited to low-dimensional synthetic toy benchmarks (2D Gaussian mixtures and concentric circles with sample sizes as small as n=20 to 50 per group). There is no validation on real-world matching or assignment datasets (e.g., school choice, labor matching, or benchmark recommender datasets).

The uniform deviation bound in Theorem 4.4 incurs an exponential factor exp(5 R_\Theta / \epsilon), which makes the theoretical guarantee very loose for moderately small regularization parameters \epsilon.

The cost learning approach lacks evaluation regarding geometric distortion: when optimizing the bilevel objective with high fairness requirements, it is unclear to what degree the learned metric deforms the original feature space and pairwise affinities.

Formatting and editorial issues are present: Sections 5.1 and 5.2 share identical duplicate headings ('Approaches and Metrics') on page 10, and multiple broken citation placeholders ('[? ]') appear in Section C of the appendix.

strengths: The paper formulates an intuitive and practically relevant group fairness framework for matching problems within entropic optimal transport, moving beyond individual fairness notions to central-planner quotas.

The presentation explores multiple operational regimes: exact enforcement via an alternating projection algorithm, a convex relaxation via penalization, and an inductive formulation via metric/cost learning.

The statistical analysis provides rigorous non-asymptotic bounds, establishing an expected estimation rate of order n^{-1/2} for the penalized entropic objective without sacrificing the standard convergence rate of entropic OT.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is restricted to low-dimensional synthetic benchmarks (2D Gaussian mixtures and concentric rings) with very small sample sizes (around 20 samples per subgroup). Validating the framework on realistic matching or allocation datasets is necessary to demonstrate practical utility.

The deviation guarantee for the cost learning framework (Theorem 4.4) bounds the expectation for fixed parameters before taking a supremum over the parameter set, rather than providing uniform control over data-dependent parameters selected by empirical optimization. As a result, it does not fully characterize true generalization for the learned cost function.

Several formatting and editorial defects detract from the quality of the submission, including duplicated subsections (Sections 5.1 and 5.2 share identical text and headers), broken citations marked with question marks in Appendix C, and overlapping text and tabular elements within Figure 7.

The novelty of the algorithmic tools is somewhat incremental, as FairSinkhorn directly specializes classical iterative Bregman projections for affine constraints, and the penalized solver relies on existing generalized conditional gradient algorithms.

strengths: Original and well-motivated problem formulation: Enforcing group fairness directly on the optimal transport coupling via predefined target inter-group mass distributions is conceptually clean, practically relevant (e.g., in resource allocation, school assignment, and recommendation systems), and distinct from prior work that mostly uses OT merely as a downstream tool for fair representation learning.

Comprehensive methodology: The paper provides a clear spectrum of solutions, ranging from exact fairness (FairSinkhorn) to two well-reasoned relaxations (convex penalized OT and reusable bilevel cost learning).

Rigorous theoretical analysis: The authors establish strong finite-sample guarantees, specifically an O(n^{-1/2}) sample complexity bound for fairness-penalized entropic OT (Theorem 4.2) and a uniform deviation bound for out-of-sample fairness in the cost-learning setting (Theorem 4.4).

Clear writing and convincing empirical verification: The manuscript is well structured and clearly presented. The empirical evaluation systematically evaluates the fairness-cost trade-offs, inference time improvements, convergence behavior, and performance on both synthetic distributions and a semi-synthetic real-world matching problem.
weaknesses: Lack of convergence guarantee for FairSinkhorn: While Proposition 3.3 derives the first-order optimality condition for the exact problem, Algorithm 1 alternatingly rescales the dual potentials. The manuscript demonstrates empirical convergence in Figure 7a, but does not provide a formal proof that this multi-marginal/three-way alternating projection scheme is guaranteed to converge to the optimum.

Exponential constant in regularization parameter: In Theorem 4.4, the bound contains an exp(5 R_\Theta / \epsilon) factor. While this dependence is known to arise in worst-case entropic OT bounds, it makes the theoretical bound loose/vacuous for small regularization parameters \epsilon.

Scale of experiments: The empirical validations are primarily conducted on relatively small synthetic problems (e.g., sample sizes of 25 to 1000) and a semi-synthetic dataset. Demonstrating scalability on larger-scale matching benchmarks would further strengthen the practical claims.

strengths: Novel and timely problem formulation: while existing literature predominantly applies optimal transport as an auxiliary tool for fair representation or fair classification, this paper addresses group fairness on the transport plan itself, which directly reflects real-world matching problems (e.g., school assignment, dating apps, hiring).

Comprehensive algorithmic framework: the paper provides both an exact formulation with an efficient modified Sinkhorn algorithm (FairSinkhorn) and two principled relaxation strategies (convex penalization and bilevel cost learning) that navigate the fairness-transport cost trade-off.

Rigorous theoretical analysis: the authors prove finite-sample complexity bounds of rate $O(n^{-1/2})$ for the fairness-penalized entropic OT problem (Theorem 4.2) and a uniform deviation bound for out-of-sample generalization under learned costs (Theorem 4.4).

High practical relevance of the cost-learning formulation: framing cost learning to induce fair matchings allows reusing the learned metric on unseen samples without resolving expensive constrained optimization problems from scratch.
Clear presentation and thorough experimental validation on both synthetic distributions and semi-synthetic matching datasets, supported by complete proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: Lack of formal convergence proof for Algorithm 1 (FairSinkhorn): while the derivation of the first-order optimality condition (Proposition 3.3) is sound and empirical convergence matches Sinkhorn, the manuscript does not provide a formal proof of convergence (e.g., establishing it as block coordinate ascent on the dual or cyclic Bregman projection) for this 3-way alternating scaling.

Heuristic nature of the semi-synthetic dataset construction: the dating app experiments rely on hand-crafted distance metrics (e.g., arbitrary distance penalties for mismatched locations and orientations) and synthetically imputed target couplings; evaluating on an authentic bipartite assignment benchmark (such as public school choice or labor clearinghouse records) would further solidify practical validity.

Minor notation and typesetting inconsistencies in the proofs: in Theorem 4.2, Equation (12) contains a typo stating $O(1/\sqrt{n}^{-1})$ instead of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$, and in Section 4.2 / Appendix C.3 there are occasional notation slips between indices ($B_{uv}$ vs. $B_{sw}$ and $F_{sv}$ vs. $F_{sw}$).

strengths: Original and well-motivated conceptual perspective: Enforcing group-level fairness constraints directly on the optimal transport plan (coupling) addresses an important gap in the literature, which has largely used OT as a tool for fair representations or fair barycenters rather than constraining the matching itself.

Comprehensive suite of algorithms: The paper covers the exact constraint setting via FairSinkhorn (a multi-marginal/iterative scaling projection algorithm), a relaxed convex penalization approach solved via generalized conditional gradient, and a parametric cost-learning approach via bilevel optimization for out-of-sample generalization.

Rigorous theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.2 establishes an $O(n^{-1/2})$ sample complexity bound for the penalized entropic OT problem via a non-trivial sandwiching technique and linearization of the fairness penalty. Theorem 4.4 provides explicit finite-sample deviation bounds for the cost-learning objective.

Clear writing and balanced empirical evaluation: The paper is clearly presented, provides intuitive low-dimensional illustrations (Gaussians and concentric circles), compares linear vs. expressive non-linear costs, and includes an application to semi-synthetic dating app data.
weaknesses: Lack of a formal convergence proof for FairSinkhorn: While Proposition 3.3 derives the first-order optimality condition of the dual formulation, the paper does not provide a theoretical convergence proof or contraction rate for the cyclic three-way scaling updates in Algorithm 1. Although empirical convergence is observed in Appendix D.5, establishing convergence for generalized multi-marginal / non-standard Bregman projections typically requires formal contraction arguments (e.g., in Hilbert's projective metric).

Nature of the generalization bound in Theorem 4.4: In Theorem 4.4, the statement bounds $\sup_{\theta \in \Theta} \mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{L}_F(\Pi_\epsilon(c_\theta)) - \mathcal{L}_F(\pi^\star_\epsilon(c_\theta))|]$, which is a pointwise-in-$\theta$ bound with a uniform constant rather than a uniform empirical process bound $\mathbb{E}[\sup_{\theta \in \Theta} |\dots|]$. Because the parameter $\hat{\theta}_n$ is learned from data, guaranteeing that the learned cost achieves low population fairness loss requires uniform control over $\Theta$ (e.g., via Rademacher complexity or metric entropy of the cost class).

Modeling limitations of entropic OT for matching markets: While OT offers computational tractability, real-world matching problems (e.g., school choice, labor markets, dating apps) are typically one-to-one or one-to-many non-fractional assignments where two-sided preferences and stability (absence of blocking pairs) are paramount. Entropic OT yields soft, fractional couplings, and while deterministic sampling is discussed, the trade-off between fairness and stability is left unaddressed.
